analysis.one_liner: Admits Washington, D.C. as a state with two senators and one House member.
analysis.headline: Introduced January 9, 2025 with 43 of the Senate's 47 Democrats and independents as cosponsors; it was referred to committee the same day and has received no further action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make most of the District of Columbia the State of Washington, Douglass Commonwealth, giving its roughly 700,000 residents two senators and one voting House member. A smaller federal enclave containing the Capitol, White House, Supreme Court, and monuments would remain the seat of the national government under congressional control. Current D.C. laws, courts, and contracts would carry over, and a commission would manage the transition.
analysis.who_benefits: The residents of the District of Columbia, who currently pay federal taxes and serve in the military but have no voting senators or representative. Under the bill, they would elect two senators and one House member, and their local government would become a state government rather than a entity Congress can override. Residents of the remaining federal enclave could vote absentee in the state where they last lived.

how_it_helps.text: Grants the District of Columbia full statehood on equal footing with the other states, with two senators and one House member, while carving out a smaller federal 'Capital' containing the Capitol, White House, Supreme Court, monuments, and adjacent federal office buildings as the seat of government.

Carries over existing D.C. laws, courts, contracts, and pending cases into the new state, and keeps federal obligations for judges' retirement, the public defender service, and prisoner housing until the state certifies it can take them over.

Lets residents of the remaining federal Capital vote absentee in federal elections in the state of their most recent prior residence, and repeals the D.C. Delegate office once a voting representative exists.
Bars the new state from taxing federal property except as Congress permits, and reserves federal authority over defense and Coast Guard lands within the state.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would cover the transition and some continuing obligations, such as the judges' retirement fund, until the state certifies it has funds and laws to assume them. The state would take on those obligations over time. The federal government would also continue to maintain the enlarged federal enclave.

drawbacks.text: Constitutional questions are the strongest objection. The Constitution assigns electoral votes to the federal district, so the bill pairs statehood with fast-tracked procedures for a constitutional amendment repealing the 23rd Amendment; critics argue admission by ordinary statute cannot be squared with the Constitution's treatment of the seat of government, and the bill itself is written to be non-severable, meaning a court ruling against one admission provision could invalidate the whole act.

The federal seat of government shrinks but does not disappear: Congress keeps a standing federal district, the new state cannot tax federal property within it, and Congress retains authority over defense lands inside the state, which some argue leaves a hybrid arrangement rather than a clean separation.

The state assumes real fiscal obligations over time, including the judges' retirement program and the public defender service, once it certifies it has the funding and laws in place; that shifts costs now borne federally onto the new state's taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For D.C. residents, the gain is fundamental: full voting representation and self-government for a population larger than several existing states. The administrative costs of transition are modest and mostly borne by the federal government initially. The serious risks are legal rather than fiscal, since the constitutional challenge to statehood-by-statute is likely to be litigated, and the bill's non-severability clause makes the whole act vulnerable if courts side with challengers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled since.

narrative.text: Senator Van Hollen introduced S. 51 on January 9, 2025, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day.
The bill has 43 cosponsors: 42 of the Senate's 45 Democrats and 1 of its 2 independents. No Republican has cosponsored.
The action history shows no action after the January 9 referral; the bill has not been scheduled for a committee markup or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of D.C. statehood, who keep the Senate and House composition unchanged and retain the current arrangement under which Congress controls D.C. laws and its residents lack voting representation. D.C. residents remain without senators or a voting House member.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Statehood opponents; the Senate stays unchanged

for.name: Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Washington, D.C. Admission Act in the Senate on January 9, 2025.

for.name: 42 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it the position of nearly the entire Democratic caucus.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Rand Paul
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a committee markup or hearing; the bill has sat in committee since its January 9, 2025 referral.

against.name: 55 of 55 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 55 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill, leaving it without any Republican support in a chamber Republicans hold 55 seats.

sides.party_line_note: 43 of the Senate's 47 Democrats and independents cosponsored the bill; none of the 55 Republicans did, so support is entirely on one side of the aisle.

industries.industry: Federal government (property and seat of government)
industries.note: The bill locks in a federal Capital enclave and federal title to all federal property, bars the new state from taxing federal property, and reserves congressional authority over defense lands, so federal control of the seat of government continues even while residents around it become a state.

Statehood would add two senators and one House member from a jurisdiction whose electorate votes overwhelmingly for one party, shifting the chamber's balance. That is the concentrated interest at stake in who advances or blocks the bill, alongside the representation question for residents.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 Senate seats and the committee chair having taken no action since the January 2025 referral, the bill is very likely to remain in committee without a markup, hearing, or floor vote for the rest of this Congress, the same path similar D.C. statehood bills have followed in recent Congresses.
